strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing 3DGS SLAM systems are almost entirely purely visual, and the paper delivers one of the first tightly coupled RGB+IMU Gaussian Splatting SLAM systems that jointly optimizes poses, disparities, and IMU states within a unified optimization framework.

Very extensive experimental evidence: four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2) spanning indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot captures, with 13 baselines across classic VI-SLAM, learned SLAM, and GS-SLAM families. VIGS-SLAM achieves the best or near-best ATE in almost all settings (e.g., 2.79 cm avg on EuRoC vs. 4.30 cm for ORB-SLAM3) and consistently better rendering metrics than the strongest visual GS baselines.

Careful and fair evaluation practices: metrics reported for online performance before final global BA/color refinement (with both variants provided in supplementary), rendering evaluated only on non-keyframe views, Recall metrics introduced to avoid ATE being misleading under failure, and an honest breakdown of where copied-vs-reproduced baseline numbers come from.

Meaningful robustness analysis: strided evaluations simulating frame drops, and a self-captured extreme-condition sequence, showing the practical value of IMU coupling rather than just benchmark average gains.

Reasonable ablations covering the three key design choices (IMU fusion, loop closure, IMU-based keyframe initialization) and the loop-closure Gaussian update, plus a runtime analysis with clear hardware specification.

Honest limitations section (no multi-camera/fisheye support, high-end GPU requirement) and a clear system description; judged as an Applied/Systems contribution, the integration quality and empirical rigor are appropriate evidence for the claims.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative: the visual front-end, vision residuals, and dense BA layer follow DROID-SLAM; the PGBA loop-closure scheme is inspired by HI-SLAM2; IMU preintegration residuals and staged initialization follow established VIO practice (Forster et al., VINS-Mono). The technical novelty over VINGS-Mono/MM3DGS-SLAM (joint windowed visual-inertial optimization, time-varying biases, Jacobian-corrected preintegration, consistent Gaussian updates) is real but incremental, and the paper does not isolate what is algorithmically new versus re-engineered.

The 'real-time' claim in the abstract is questionable: supplementary Table 9 shows ~16 FPS for tracking alone and ~7 FPS for the full system on an RTX 5090, below the 20-30 Hz frame rates of the datasets, and the authors admit part of the IMU code is unoptimized NumPy. The system is not clearly real-time as presented.

Some baseline comparisons are weaker than ideal: EuRoC numbers for several classic baselines are copied from the ORB-SLAM3 paper, DROID-SLAM numbers from its paper, and MM3DGS-SLAM (the only directly comparable VI-GS method) is evaluated only on UTMM with results copied from its paper because the code does not support RGB+IMU. A stronger head-to-head against a reproduced VI-GS baseline would substantially strengthen the VI-specific claims.

FAST-LIVO2 'ground truth' is itself an odometry estimate (LiDAR-inertial-visual pseudo GT), and the extreme-condition sequence also uses FAST-LIVO2 pseudo GT; errors on these datasets could partly reflect GT artifacts, and this caveat is not explicitly discussed. Similarly, the self-captured extreme sequence has only qualitative, single-sequence evidence.

Loop closure detection is based on simple optical-flow magnitude and relative-angle heuristics rather than established place-recognition descriptors; false-positive loop behavior is not analyzed, and several thresholds (τkf, τLC-flow, τLC-ang, τinit) appear dataset-sensitive, though the authors claim shared hyperparameters across datasets.

Reproducibility concerns: the project page link in the abstract is empty, code release is not committed, and critical initialization equations are deferred to the supplementary; IMU-related components are admittedly not fully optimized, so reimplementation would be difficult.

Minor clarity issues: typo in Eq. 4 ('Lios'), the loop-closure Gaussian update and IMU initialization receive somewhat terse treatments, and the motivation for design choices (e.g., the 3-second forced keyframe interval trading keyframe count for drift) is only partially analyzed.

strengths: Extensive evaluation: four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2), 13 baselines, ablations for tracking, mapping, and initialization, plus strided-robustness evaluation with a sensible Recall metric that exposes ATE's blind spot on partial trajectories (well argued in the supplementary).

The system-level integration is competent: staged IMU initialization (vision-only -> inertial-only with log-scale -> joint), uncertainty-gated keyframe initialization, and the batched analytic Gaussian update after pose-graph BA (Eqs. 5-7) is a practical and clearly described mechanism for maintaining map consistency after loop closure.

Largely honest reporting: results are given both before and after global BA/color refinement, failures of baselines are marked, and unfair comparisons (MM3DGS-SLAM protocol mismatch) are explicitly flagged rather than hidden.
The strided evaluation protocol is a genuinely useful addition and the supplementary per-sequence tables (Tables 19-20) show the work needed to support robustness claims.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The system is essentially DROID-SLAM with standard Forster-style IMU preintegration residuals appended (Eq. 2 is textbook VINS-Mono/OKVIS material), plus PGBA loop closure borrowed from HI-SLAM2 and a Gaussian map update. The claims of 'jointly optimizing visual and inertial energy terms' vs. prior work's 'naive pairwise' fusion are not backed by any analysis showing why the formulation differs substantively from VI-BA as practiced for a decade. No new algorithmic idea is clearly attributable to this paper.

The 'real-time' claim is overstated. Table 9 shows ~7 FPS for the full system on an RTX 5090 at 848x480, slower than HI-SLAM2's ~12.5 FPS; the supplementary admits part of the IMU code is unoptimized NumPy. Tracking-only at ~16 FPS barely qualifies. A runtime-oriented systems claim should be measured on more typical hardware and stated accurately in the abstract.

Ground-truth validity concerns on the headline outdoor results: FAST-LIVO2-dataset 'ground truth' is FAST-LIVO2's own LiDAR-inertial output, and the self-captured 'extreme conditions' sequence also uses FAST-LIVO2 pseudo-GT. Evaluating against pseudo-GT from a method that itself fails on the same challenging conditions circularizes the comparison; error bars/confidence on this pseudo-GT are unquantified.

Loop closure detection is crude and heuristic: an optical-flow magnitude threshold plus a 120-degree orientation gate with a fixed 55-keyframe gap is far weaker than standard BoW/learned retrieval, and the paper provides no precision/recall analysis of loop detection despite loop closure being one of its main claimed contributions.

Comparison fairness is uneven: several EuRoC baseline numbers are copied from the ORB-SLAM3 paper under different protocols, MM3DGS-SLAM numbers are copied from its paper, and rendering comparisons are only against two visual-only systems since the VI baselines produce no maps. The EuRoC average margin over HI-SLAM2 (2.79 vs 2.94 cm) is small and within plausible run-to-run variance for reproduced baselines.

Robustness claims need qualification: in the strided evaluation the method also collapses at stride 20-40 (e.g., 300.79 cm ATE on strided EuRoC at stride 40, similar to HI-SLAM2), so the framing that it 'remains stable' applies only to moderate degradation.

Presentation issues: empty 'Project page:' link in the abstract, a typo in Eq. 4 (L_{ios}), hyperparameter thresholds (tau_kf=2.4, tau_LC-flow=22, etc.) presented without sensitivity analysis, and key details of inertial-only initialization deferred to the supplementary rather than the main text.

No code release is stated, and given that the paper positions itself against 'preprints with limited code availability,' reproducibility is a concern for a systems paper whose contribution is largely engineering integration.

strengths: Strong and comprehensive empirical evaluation: four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2) spanning indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot capture, with comparisons to 13 baselines including classical VI-SLAM, visual 3DGS SLAM, and feed-forward methods. VIGS-SLAM is consistently first or near-first in ATE and best in rendering quality (Tables 1-5).

The system design is technically sound: a genuinely tightly coupled formulation that jointly optimizes visual and inertial residuals (Eq. 1-2) with per-keyframe bias estimation, Jacobian-based online correction of IMU preintegration, a staged IMU initialization, and Sim(3) pose-graph bundle adjustment. This addresses documented weaknesses of prior VI-3DGS attempts (pairwise constraints, fixed bias, decoupled optimization).

The loop-closure Gaussian update (Eqs. 5-7) is an elegant, efficient mechanism to keep the map globally consistent without re-optimizing all Gaussians, and its benefit is demonstrated both qualitatively and in the ablation (Tables 6-7, 17).

Robustness evaluation is a valuable addition beyond standard ATE benchmarks: strided evaluations with Recall metrics expose ATE's blind spots (e.g., a method achieving low ATE while tracking only a short segment), plus an extreme-condition self-captured sequence. Honest reporting of online results before final BA/refinement, with refined results in the supplementary, supports reproducibility and fair comparison.
Detailed supplementary material (dataset statistics, hyperparameters, runtime analysis, full per-sequence results before/after refinement) substantially strengthens transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily integrative: the visual front-end, dense BA, and residual formulation build directly on DROID-SLAM, PGBA is inspired by HI-SLAM2, and the mapping/loss design follows MonoGS. The individual technical components (preintegration, bias smoothness, staged initialization) are well-established; the contribution is their careful unification rather than fundamentally new machinery. This should be stated more explicitly against the strong novelty claims in the introduction.

The 'real-time' claim is only marginally supported: full-system runtime is ~7 FPS (tracking+mapping) on an RTX 5090, and as low as ~4 FPS on some sequences, while FAST-LIVO2 input is 10 FPS. The authors acknowledge unoptimized NumPy IMU code, but the paper headline ('robust real-time tracking') slightly oversells current performance.

Some evaluation aspects weaken confidence: FAST-LIVO2 ground truth is itself pseudo-GT from another odometry system; the extreme-conditions sequence is a single self-captured clip with pseudo-GT (Sec. 4.2); MM3DGS-SLAM results are partially copied from its paper under a non-comparable rendering protocol; and loop-closure detection relies on hand-tuned optical-flow/angle thresholds (tau_LC-flow, tau_LC-ang) that may not generalize.

The strided results at higher strides undermine the robustness narrative to some degree: at stride 20/40 the proposed method also degrades severely or fails on most sequences (Tables 19-20, e.g., average recall@10cm of ~29% at stride 20 on RPNG). The method degrades more gracefully than baselines, but 'remains stable' in Sec. 4.2 is somewhat overstated.

Method exposition has gaps: the inertial-only initialization step is deferred to the supplementary, the fallback threshold tau and gravity/scale recovery are given only at the level of equations, and there is no analysis of sensitivity to IMU noise characteristics or calibration errors, which is central for a VI system.
Two 'd) Visual Inertial Gaussian Splatting SLAM' category labels in Sec. 4 and minor typographical issues (e.g., 'Lios' in Eq. 4) suggest a final polish pass is needed.
